title: Type erasure: compiler erases generics, consequences: no new T(), no instanceof List<String>, bridge methods
keyPoints: Type erasure means the Java compiler removes all generic type parameters after compile-time checking, replacing them with their bounds or Object.
At runtime, List<String> and List<Integer> are the same class (ArrayList), with no way to distinguish them.
You cannot write new T() because the JVM does not know what T is at runtime; the workaround is passing Class<T> and using reflection.
You cannot write instanceof List<String> because type parameters are erased; use instanceof List<?> with unbounded wildcard instead.
You cannot create a generic exception class (class MyException<T> extends Exception) because catch clauses need concrete types.
Bridge methods are synthetic methods the compiler generates to preserve polymorphism after erasure, bridging erased and specific signatures.
Type erasure was chosen for backward compatibility with pre-Java-5 code: generic and raw collections interoperate seamlessly.

s1_definition.oneliner: Type erasure means the Java compiler enforces generic type safety at compile time and then removes all type parameters from the bytecode, so at runtime List<String> and List<Integer> are both just List.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Erasure process** – the compiler replaces `T` with `Object` (or the upper bound if bounded: `T extends Number` becomes `Number`), inserts casts where needed, and generates bridge methods
- **Same class at runtime** – `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` are both `ArrayList` at runtime; `list.getClass()` returns the same Class object
- **Restrictions** – no `new T()`, no `instanceof T`, no `T.class`, no generic exception types, no generic array creation (`new T[]`)
- **Bridge methods** – synthetic methods generated to maintain polymorphism when a subclass narrows a type parameter; they delegate from the erased signature to the specific one
- **Backward compatibility** – erasure ensures that generic code interoperates with pre-Java-5 raw type code without breaking existing bytecode
s1_definition.analogy: Generics are like coloured labels on filing drawers at National Bank of India during work hours (compile time). The green label says "Savings accounts only" and the red label says "Loan documents only". The compiler uses these labels to prevent Rajesh from putting a loan document in the savings drawer. But at the end of the day (runtime), the cleaning crew rips off all labels (erasure). Every drawer just says "Files". You cannot ask "Is this the savings drawer?" because the label is gone.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Type Erasure Process
  =====================

  Source code:                     Bytecode (after erasure):
  ┌──────────────────────┐         ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ class Box<T> {       │         │ class Box {           │
  │   T item;            │ ──────▶ │   Object item;       │
  │   T get() {}         │         │   Object get() {}    │
  │   void set(T t) {}   │         │   void set(Object) {}│
  │ }                    │         │ }                    │
  └──────────────────────┘         └──────────────────────┘

  Box<String> b = new Box<>();     Box b = new Box();
  String s = b.get();              String s = (String) b.get();
                                   // compiler inserts cast

  Bridge Method:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ interface Comparable<T> { int compareTo(T o); }      │
  │ After erasure: int compareTo(Object o)               │
  │                                                       │
  │ class Account implements Comparable<Account> {        │
  │   int compareTo(Account o) { ... }                   │
  │   int compareTo(Object o) { return compareTo((Account)o); } │
  │                            ^^^^ bridge method (synthetic)    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Type erasure is the mechanism by which Java generics provide compile-time type safety without changing the runtime bytecode format. The compiler checks all type constraints, inserts necessary casts, and then removes all type parameters. At runtime, List<String> and List<Integer> are the same class, and there is no way to distinguish them.

This creates several restrictions: you cannot write new T() (the JVM does not know what T is), you cannot use instanceof with parameterised types, you cannot create generic arrays, and you cannot create generic exception classes. The workaround for new T() is to pass Class<T> and use reflection. Bridge methods are generated automatically to preserve polymorphism when a class narrows a generic type parameter.

At National Bank of India, Rajesh's generic Repository<T> pattern could not do new T() to create empty entity instances. Instead, the repository constructor accepted Class<T>, and the factory method used reflection. This is the standard pattern used by JPA repositories, Spring Data, and similar frameworks.

Remember one sentence: type erasure removes all generic type information at compile time for backward compatibility, making List<String> and List<Integer> the same class at runtime, which is why you cannot do new T() or instanceof List<String>.
